_work.title: Compendium Maleficarum — Guazzo's Demonological Woodcut Cycle (1608/1626)
_work.blurb: The visual compendium of early modern witchcraft iconography. Francesco Maria Guazzo's *Compendium Maleficarum* (first edition Milan 1608; second edition Milan 1626) is a Dominican friar's systematic demonological treatise illustrated by a cycle of 22 engraved woodcuts that constituted the most comprehensive and widely reproduced visual catalogue of witchcraft practices in the early modern period. Unlike the earlier *Malleus Maleficarum* (1486), which had no illustrations, Guazzo's work presented each category of diabolical act — the pact with the Devil, the mark, apostasy, the sabbath with dancing and feasting, weather magic, killing cattle, flight by broomstick and on animals, transformation, harmful magic and maleficium — as a distinct engraved scene. The woodcuts drew on the accumulated tradition of witch imagery established by Hans Baldung Grien (1510), Dürer (1498–1500), and the artist of the *Champion des Dames* (c. 1451), but systematized that tradition into a numbered demonological typology directly keyed to the text's chapter structure. The 1626 edition reproduced the same woodcut cycle as 1608 with minor variations. Guazzo's work was compiled during the height of the witch trials and was used as an authority in Italian, Spanish, and German courts. The woodcuts became the canonical visual reference for sabbath, pact, and maleficium iconography in subsequent demonological literature and persist as the primary visual source for academic study of early modern witchcraft belief.

entries.summary:
A composite photograph showing all 22 woodcut engravings from Francesco Maria Guazzo's *Compendium Maleficarum* (Milan, 1608), the most comprehensive visual typology of witchcraft practices produced in the early modern period. The 22 scenes are arranged in a grid, each depicting a distinct category of diabolical act as classified by Guazzo's three-book demonological treatise.

## Iconography

The 22 woodcuts form a systematic visual encyclopaedia of the pact-sabbath-maleficium triad that structured early modern witchcraft belief. Scene 1: the Pact — a witch kneels before the Devil (depicted in hybrid human-bestial form) and signs the diabolical contract with blood or pen; the Devil places his hand on the witch's shoulder. Scene 2: Renunciation of Baptism — the witch formally abjures Christian faith. Scene 3: the Devil's Mark — a demon or Devil applies the infamous *stigma diabolicum* to the witch's body, often the back, shoulder, or hidden areas; later magistrates would probe for this insensible mark during trials. Scene 4: the Devil's Kiss (*osculum infame*) — the witch kisses the Devil's posterior in a ceremony of diabolical submission. Scene 5–8: Witches' Sabbath preparations — robing in animal skins, receiving unguents from the Devil, smearing broomstick or pitchfork with flying ointment. Scenes 9–12: the Flight — witches fly through the night air on broomsticks, shovels, pitchforks, and on the backs of animals (goat, ram). Scenes 13–15: the Sabbath assembly — witches dancing back-to-back in a ring with the Devil presiding, feasting at the sabbath table, sexual intercourse with incubi/succubi. Scenes 16–18: Weather magic — witches boiling a cauldron to raise storms, striking cattle dead with cursed wands. Scenes 19–22: Maleficium — witches poisoning individuals and animals, digging up corpses for body-part ingredients, causing impotence and disease through magical objects buried at thresholds.

## Significance

Guazzo's woodcut cycle is the pivotal visual document in the history of the sabbath concept. By 1608 the major components of the accumulated sabbath image — the night flight, the assembly, the pact with the Devil, the inverted Christian rites — had been codified through a century of demonological writing (Institoris and Sprenger's *Malleus Maleficarum* 1486, Bodin's *De la Démonomanie* 1580, del Río's *Disquisitionum Magicarum* 1599–1600), but Guazzo was the first to give these concepts a comprehensive, numbered visual form. Charles Zika's fundamental study (*The Appearance of Witchcraft*, 2007) demonstrates how Guazzo's woodcuts built on and systematized the previous century of witch imagery in German and Flemish prints — particularly Baldung Grien's *Witches' Sabbath* (1510), Dürer's *Witch Riding Backwards* (c.1500), and the Flemish sabbath compositions. Stuart Clark (*Thinking with Demons*, 1997) places the Guazzo imagery within the epistemological framework of inversion and the *mundus inversus* that structured demonological thought: each Guazzo woodcut visualizes a deliberate parody or inversion of a Christian sacrament (pact = baptism inverted; sabbath feast = Eucharist inverted; osculum infame = reverence inverted). Lyndal Roper (*Witch Craze*, 2004) and Brian Levack (*The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe*, 2016) situate the Guazzo imagery within the social and psychological context of early modern confessions obtained under torture, which projected fantasies of sexual disorder, cannibalism, and social inversion onto accused witches — fantasies that Guazzo's woodcuts reified and circulated. The composite photograph used for this entry was made from the original 1608 copper plates photographed through photogrammetric reconstruction, providing unusually sharp detail of all 22 scenes simultaneously.

## For artists & game designers

Guazzo's 22 scenes constitute the definitive visual toolkit for early modern witchcraft iconography: every major category of sabbath activity, maleficium, and diabolical pact is here, precisely labelled by the demonological tradition. The flight scenes (broomstick, pitchfork, goat, ram) are the primary historical source for the witch-flight image that entered popular culture. The pact scene is the model for almost all subsequent diabolical-contract imagery in Western art. The witch's mark scene is essential for understanding historical trial procedures and their visual representation in broadsheets.
